parole.testo: From Middle Dutch becken, from Vulgar Latin *baccinum. Doublet of bassin.

From Middle Dutch cassiede, cautsiede, calsijde and other variants (predominantly used in Flanders and the Southern regions of the Netherlands), all meaning “paved road”, from Vulgar Latin (via) calciāta (“paved road”). Cognate with English causey and causeway, from the same source.

From Middle Dutch keper (“rafter, roof beam”), from Vulgar Latin *capriōne, *capreus, from Latin caper (“male goat”). The connection with goats is thought to be the resemblance of two diagonal wooden beams of a roof meeting in the middle with two prancing goats. Cognate with Middle High German kepfe

parole.significato: a cherry tree, one of certain trees of the genus Prunus, especially the subgenus Cerasus
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch kerse, ultimately from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin.

parole.significato: the bird species Calidris canutus (syn. Tringa canutis)
parole.testo: From the cognate English knot, possibly influenced by Vulgar Latin canutus (“grey-headed", "grizzled”).
From Middle Dutch mêester, from Old Dutch *mēster, from Vulgar Latin *maester, from Latin magister.
From Middle Dutch mennen, from Old Dutch *mennen, borrowed via Vulgar Latin from Latin mināre, collateral form of minārī.

parole.significato: a pear, a fruit of the pear tree
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch pēre, from Vulgar Latin *pira, from Latin pirum.
From Middle Dutch sarc, serc, from Vulgar Latin *sarcus, from Latin sarcophagus, from Ancient Greek σαρκοφάγος (sarkophágos).
From Middle Dutch pijler, pijlre, from Vulgar Latin *pīlāre, either directly or via Middle Low German piler. Doublet of pilaar, which is a later borrowing from Medieval Latin.
